extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reviewers assessing submissions to ICLR 2019, covering publication standards (novelty, interest, rigor), topic fit, anonymity, length limits, handling concurrent submissions, and prior-work (arXiv) policy. Intended to guide accept/reject recommendations and reviewer conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication standards — novelty and contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper present substantively new ideas or explore an underexplored or highly novel question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should value papers that take risks and study less-explored areas (which may have less polished results) and not excessively penalize them. Conversely, papers presenting state-of-the-art results on well-studied problems should be considered if they substantively advance the state of the art. Ask whether a substantial fraction of ICLR attendees will be interested and whether you would send the paper to a colleague to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest / relevance to the ICLR community
rubrics_metrics.description: Will a substantial fraction of the ICLR attendees be interested in reading this paper?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use community interest as part of acceptability. The heuristic 'would I send this paper to one of my colleagues to read?' is recommended as an indicator, though not the only one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific rigor and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a high standard in terms of scientific rigor: evaluations/validation, proofs, and other substantive arguments must be correct and convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you believe a paper has flaws in evaluation, validation, proofs, or other discussion, explicitly point them out to authors. Authors will have a chance to address concerns; reviewers play a role in iterative improvement. Verify necessary details for reproducibility or proof correctness, which may be in appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness to novel/risky work
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for variation in polish between risky/underexplored work and well-studied-topic papers when judging quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that papers exploring new areas may have less polished results; avoid excessively penalizing them simply for lack of polish. Apply judgment to weigh novelty and potential impact versus current maturity of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic fit / scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper within the scope of ICLR's topics?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICLR covers a large segment of machine learning research and applications; if uncertain about fit, contact your area chair. Topic fit questions can be raised with the AC rather than being treated as a hard rejection criterion by the reviewer alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity / double-blind requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: ICLR is double-blind: authors do not know reviewer identities and reviewers do not know author identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you believe a paper contains an anonymity violation, contact your AC immediately. Anonymity violations are requirements for submission and are not part of the scientific review criteria. Unless the AC rules otherwise, proceed to review normally. Do not reveal your or the authors' identities in discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length and page-limit expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended main-text length is 8 pages; strict upper limit of 10 pages. Unlimited additional pages allowed for citations and appendices (appendices must come after the bibliography).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are not required to read all appendices, but details necessary for reproducibility or to validate proofs may be in appendices — reviewers should verify they are present and correct if concerned about reproducibility/correctness. Encourage authors to avoid overly lengthy papers; reviewers may apply a higher reviewing standard to papers that substantially exceed typical length. If a paper is too lengthy, point this out to authors to allow revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices and reproducibility expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may include unlimited appendices after the bibliography; necessary details for reproducibility or proofs may be there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While reviewers are not obligated to read every appendix, they must check that information required to assess reproducibility or correctness exists and is correct when relevant. Treat appendices as acceptable places for extended details but verify their sufficiency when those details are material to your evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar / concurrent submissions handling
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple concurrent submissions on similar topics appear, they should be reviewed to the same standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you believe there is another ICLR submission that is concurrent and similar to the one you are reviewing, contact your AC so the situation can be addressed. Ensure fairness across concurrent submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: ArXiv and prior-work policy
rubrics_metrics.description: ICLR considers unpublished arXiv papers to be prior work under a minimum standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No paper will be considered prior work if it appeared on arXiv (or another online venue) less than 30 days prior to the ICLR deadline. Reviewers should apply reasonable community standards for what constitutes prior work, but the 30-day minimum is enforced.
